profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized asset management firm between the Quant Research Lead and the Product Strategy Manager to prepare a narrowly scoped internal rollout package for a new portfolio construction capability based on portfolio optimization under a correlation constraint. The capability uses a multiperiod market model with one tradable stock, stochastic income, and a non-tradable index, and compares constrained subgame perfect (CSGP) and constrained precommitment (CPC) strategies against an unconstrained case. The firm wants to decide what will be included in a 'bare-bones MVP' for next week's investment committee discussion, how the annual correlation-constraint story will be demonstrated, what the 'baseline comparison' will contain, and how the small utility loss will be explained in committee materials. The agenda is to lock scope, assign ownership for the model note and committee deck, and set a timeline for draft outputs. The expected outcome is a concrete plan for a minimal committee package with clear owners, a benchmark demonstration, and agreed talking points that each participant believes are fully aligned.

members.name: Maya Chen
members.expertise: portfolio optimization, stochastic control, and translating academic asset-allocation models into production research frameworks
members.background: PhD in financial mathematics; previously built hedging and allocation models for insurance and retirement products; now leads quantitative research efforts that adapt mathematically tractable portfolio methods for internal investment platforms.
members.private_state: Wants the committee discussion to stay tightly bounded around the analytically solved model so she does not trigger demands for new derivations, extra calibrations, or client-facing interpretations that the team cannot yet defend rigorously.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bare-bones MVP' means the minimum viable research package: one fixed calibration, one benchmark horizon, and output tables, without any advisor-facing framing beyond a concise technical summary.

When people say the annual or 12-month benchmark for the correlation constraint, they are referring to the model's fixed benchmark time horizon at which terminal correlation is imposed in the derivation.
A 'baseline comparison' means the house standard calibration used in the research note, with one unconstrained benchmark against the constrained CSGP and CPC strategies.

If the committee asks to explain the utility loss, the appropriate explanation is the change in expected exponential utility under the constrained versus unconstrained solution, not a translation into client returns or dollars.
Because the research result says CSGP and CPC perform similarly, one representative calibration is enough to establish the core message for an initial review.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.expertise: investment product packaging, advisor narrative design, and commercialization planning for quantitative portfolio capabilities
members.background: Former private bank platform lead who translated complex model-portfolio features into advisor-ready launch materials; now works across product, investments, and distribution teams to frame quantitative capabilities for committee approval and pilot adoption.
members.private_state: Needs the committee to see the feature as practical and communicable, not just mathematically elegant, so he is quietly steering toward materials that can already be reused in an advisor pilot conversation without asking for another packaging cycle.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bare-bones MVP' means the smallest package that still looks usable in an advisor context: a simple deck, two intuitive examples, and a clean message rather than a purely technical prototype.
When people say annual or 12-month benchmark, they naturally mean the 12-month rolling horizon already used in advisor reporting and investment reviews.

A 'baseline comparison' means the standard client-story baseline the business uses to socialize new capabilities, usually a small set of core persona examples rather than a single research calibration.

If the committee wants the utility loss explained, they will expect an intuitive client translation such as approximate return drag, wealth impact, or trade-off framing, because 'expected exponential utility' by itself will not land outside the quant team.
If a result is intended for committee approval, even the minimal version should already resemble how it will later be described to advisors.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the committee package to a 'bare-bones MVP.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a minimal research artifact: one fixed model setup, one calibrated run, a short derivation summary, and no advisor-oriented examples or packaging requirements.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a minimal marketable package: still small, but including a simple advisor-style story and one or two intuitive use cases so the committee can picture a pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear 'bare-bones' as disciplined scoping language and believe they are reducing complexity; because neither is proposing a large build, the audience difference stays hidden inside the same phrase.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss showing the constraint at the 'annual benchmark' or in a '12-month view.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the model's specific fixed benchmark horizon where the terminal portfolio-index correlation constraint is imposed in the analytical solution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the standard 12-month rolling reporting window used in advisor materials and client portfolio reviews.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both horizons are naturally described as annual and both are perfectly normal in asset-management settings, so the shared language creates a strong but false sense of precision.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the committee deck should 'show the baseline comparison.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a single standard mathematical baseline: the house calibration comparing unconstrained, CSGP, and CPC outcomes under one income-index specification.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the standard business baseline set: a small group of default client-style cases, such as salaried professional and business owner, each illustrated against the unconstrained case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional work, 'baseline' sounds like an already settled reference point rather than a scoped deliverable; each assumes the other's baseline is simply the obvious one for this project.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'explain the utility loss'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the materials should 'explain the small utility loss' from imposing the correlation constraint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks success means accurately showing that constrained CSGP and CPC produce a modest decrease in expected exponential utility relative to the unconstrained solution, preserving the research definition of the trade-off.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks success means converting that trade-off into an intuitive client-facing quantity, such as a rough expected-return drag, wealth effect, or cost-of-protection style framing that a committee member can immediately interpret.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think they are discussing the same communication task rather than different standards of explanation; 'explain' sounds innocuous, and neither expects the other to distinguish between a formal utility statement and a practical performance translation.

Maya usually responds well to scope discipline language, so that's the safest way to start.
